summary: Describes using keys derived from an IKEv2 security association as the shared secret for OWAMP and TWAMP, which allows certificate-based key exchange and gives more operational flexibility.

eli5.summary: Two measuring devices reuse a key from an earlier secure chat instead of setting up a new one.

subtitle: Lets two network-measurement endpoints reuse a key from an existing IKEv2 security association instead of provisioning a shared passphrase.

tldr.problem: OWAMP and TWAMP secure their measurement traffic with a shared secret that operators must provision by hand on every pair of endpoints, which is laborious and error-prone at scale.
tldr.mechanism: Both endpoints derive the shared secret from their IKEv2 security association as prf(SK_d, "IPPM"), signal the choice with a new IKEv2Derived mode bit, and name the SA by putting its two SPIs in the KeyID field.
tldr.outcome: Certificate-based IKEv2 deployments can now secure OWAMP and TWAMP without separate key provisioning. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4656 and RFC 5357.

sections.title: Why O/TWAMP Needs a Better Key Source
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) measure latency, bandwidth and packet loss by sending probe packets. The RFC calls them O/TWAMP together. If the probes are unprotected, an attacker in the middle can alter timestamps and so change the measurement results.

Both protocols need the client and the server to hold a shared secret, and the existing mechanism supports only a pre-shared key. The RFC says that provisioning and managing these secrets for massive deployments takes a tremendous amount of effort and is prone to human error. Its example is measuring between an LTE Evolved Node B and a Security Gateway that already support certificates and IKEv2.

The idea is to derive the shared key from an IKEv2 security association (SA) the two endpoints already have. Then O/TWAMP can use certificate-based key exchange, and IKEv2 can manage the keys automatically. Both the TWAMP Control-Client and the Server must support IPsec for this to work, and IKEv2-derived keys SHOULD be used instead of shared secrets when O/TWAMP runs in a deployment using IKEv2.
sections.eli5: Setting a secret password on every pair of measuring devices is a chore, like writing a different locker code for every locker. This RFC lets the devices get the code from a secure chat they already had.

sections.title: How O/TWAMP Security Works Today
sections.content:
O/TWAMP uses AES-CBC for confidentiality and HMAC-SHA1 truncated to 128 bits for message authentication. The control protocol has three modes: unauthenticated, authenticated and encrypted. TWAMP adds a mixed mode, where the control connection is encrypted and the test traffic is unauthenticated. The authenticated, encrypted and mixed modes need a shared secret, usually a passphrase from which the key is derived with PBKDF2.

The Control-Client opens a TCP connection to the Server. The Server sends a Server Greeting with the Modes, Challenge, Salt, Count and MBZ fields. The client answers with a Set-Up-Response carrying the chosen Mode, a KeyID, a Token and a Client initialization vector. The Token holds a 16-octet Challenge, a 16-octet AES Session-key and a 32-octet HMAC-SHA1 Session-key, encrypted with AES-CBC. The Server then replies with a Server-Start message that carries the Server-IV.

The control keys are generated randomly by the Control-Client. The test-session keys are derived from the control keys and the 16-octet session identifier. The result is that the security root is the shared secret associated with the KeyID, which is what becomes hard to manage in large deployments.
sections.eli5: The two devices first say hello, agree on a secret code word, and then use it to scramble everything they say. The weak spot is how they got the code word in the first place.

sections.title: Deriving the Shared Key from IKEv2
sections.content:
In the authenticated, encrypted and mixed modes, the shared secret key MUST be derived from the IKEv2 SA. The RFC deliberately uses the IKEv2 SA rather than a child SA, because an IKEv2 SA can exist without any child SA. First SK_d is computed as defined in RFC 7296. Then:

Shared secret key = prf( SK_d, "IPPM" )

Here the string IPPM is encoded in ASCII and prf is a pseudorandom function.

The RFC recommends doing the derivation in the IPsec layer, so that IPsec keying material is not exposed to the O/TWAMP client. How the two layers talk is host-internal and outside its scope, though it sketches a lookup in the Security Association Database by the Server address on the client side, and a lookup by SPIs on the server side.

If both ends support IKEv2 but no IKEv2 SA exists, the client may either start one and choose the IKEv2 mode, or log an error and fall back to the older modes. Both are left to the implementation. If the SA is rekeyed or deleted, the derived key MUST keep being used until the O/TWAMP session ends.
sections.eli5: Both devices mix a secret they both already know with the word IPPM to cook up a new key. Because they follow the same recipe, they end up with the same key without ever sending it.

sections.title: Signalling the Mode in the Server Greeting
sections.content:
A Server that supports the method sets a new bit in the Modes field of its Server Greeting. The bit is called IKEv2Derived, and the Modes value extension MUST be supported when the method is used. A Control-Client that implements the method and sees this bit SHOULD reply with a Set-Up-Response that picks it. For example, it can choose the authenticated mode together with IKEv2 key derivation.

The RFC argues this causes no backwards-compatibility problems. A robust legacy client simply disregards the unknown bit. A new client can tell that a Server does not support the method, and can then choose another mode as in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. A client that supports the method but decides not to use it just behaves like a purely compatible legacy client.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a card that says it can use the shared-secret trick. Old clients ignore the card, and new clients can say yes or no.

sections.title: Naming the SA in the KeyID Field
sections.content:
The client and server must agree on which IKEv2 SA the key came from. A Security Parameter Index (SPI) identifies an SA, and an IKEv2 SA has two: SPIi and SPIr. Each SPI is 8 octets long. The client therefore puts them in the 80-octet KeyID field of the Set-Up-Response:

  • The first 8 octets MUST carry SPIi.
  • The second 8 octets MUST carry SPIr.
  • The remaining bits MUST be set to zero.

The Server MUST read the SPIs from the first 16 octets and ignore the rest of the field. Both sides can then derive the same key from the Mode value and the SPIs.

If the Server cannot find an IKEv2 SA that matches, it MUST log the event for operational management. It SHOULD also set the Accept field of the Server-Start message to the value 6, meaning it will not carry out further transactions in this control session.

The Set-Up-Response itself is otherwise unchanged. Only the meaning of the KeyID content and the Mode bit change.
sections.eli5: The client writes down which earlier secure chat the secret came from, using two ticket numbers. The server looks those numbers up. If it finds no such chat, it politely says it will not continue.

sections.title: Running Measurements Inside or Outside IPsec
sections.content:
The RFC notes that O/TWAMP packets can go inside the IPsec tunnel like ordinary user traffic, or outside it, depending on operator policy and what is being measured. That choice is independent of the key derivation.

It gives a reason to prefer O/TWAMP's own protection over IPsec protection of unauthenticated O/TWAMP. With the O/TWAMP mechanism, partial authentication of packets is possible, so the sequence number can be encrypted and authenticated before the timestamp is fetched. The receiver then gets the timestamp without a decryption step, which can improve accuracy.

Even in the unauthenticated mode, O/TWAMP packets between two IKEv2 systems SHOULD be configured to use the corresponding IPsec tunnel running over an external network.
sections.eli5: The measuring messages can travel in a protected tunnel or take the open road with their own lock. Either way, the lock for the open road comes from the same shared secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Because the key comes from the IKEv2 SA, the strength and limitations of the derivation are those of RFC 7296. The strength of a key from a Diffie-Hellman exchange depends on the strength of the group, the size of the exponent and the entropy of the random number generator. Weaknesses in keys and implementations, in particular denial-of-service attacks, are as defined in RFC 7296. The RFC adds no further security analysis of its own.
sections.eli5: The new key is only as strong as the secure chat it came from, so this RFC leans on that chat's rules.

sections.title: The TWAMP-Modes Registry
sections.content:
While writing the document the authors noticed that the TWAMP-Modes registry should describe single bit position flags in the 32-bit Modes field, not integer values. IANA reformatted the registry accordingly. Updates need IETF Review, and IANA SHOULD allocate monotonically increasing bit positions. No experimental bit positions are assigned.

The registry covers bits 0 to 6 from earlier RFCs. This RFC adds bit position 7, IKEv2Derived Mode Capability, referring to its Section 5. The new OWAMP-Modes registry is covered in RFC 7718.
sections.eli5: The modes are a row of light switches, and this RFC adds one more switch labelled for the new trick.
